scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origins of the eke (sōkē) are disputed.
Historian Edwin Burrows noted its martial character, whereas anthropologist Harley Harris Bartlett suggested agricultural roots.
The Catholic Weekly reported an origin linked to penance for the 1841 killing of Catholic priest Peter Chanel.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed to dazzle spectators and please community chiefs.
The dance has no hidden ritual purpose.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in four-person units called vaka ('boat') containing two men and two women facing each other.
Men hold long sticks (~2 meters) while women hold two short sticks (~40 cm).
Striking occurs on drum beats in four-count phrases: beat 1 top hit, beat 2 bottom hit, beat 3 top hit, beat 4 spatial transition.
Watch for Eke nou, Eke loa.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Vaka (boat) units of 4 dancers in rows; Eke nou stays within unit, Eke loa exchanges rows.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Accompanied by drum beat and vocal chanting.
Performers stand still during recited stanzas and strike sticks during refrains (such as 'sōkē' or 'hina hea').
Listen for the drum.
The pulse is 4/4.
Percussive rhythmic beating of wooden sticks striking together and hitting the ground over a driving drum pulse, punctuated by vocal group refrain chants.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Historian Edwin Burrows, anthropologist Harley Harris Bartlett, Saint Peter Chanel, Father Pierre Bataillon, Marie Nizier, and King Lavelua.
Variants include the Uvean eke from Wallis Island (performed in Suva in 1972), Futunan eke, and Tongan regional versions from Tafahi, Niuafoʻou, ʻEua, and Maʻufanga.
Developed independently in the Pacific, though sharing structural stick-striking features with English Morris dance.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright facing partner in four-person vaka unit.
Men hold one 2-meter long stick; women hold two 40-cm short sticks.
Controlled torso orientation facing partners or shifting diagonally.

narration: Count: 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 (eight counts, two bars). The meter is 4/4.
Rhythm pattern: Steady drum beat driving 4-count stick-striking refrains alternated with un-struck vocal verses..

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Form a four-person vaka with two men facing two women.
Step 2: Stand stationary during the recited vocal stanzas.
Footwork from the sources: Transitions and turns performed on the 4th beat of each stick-striking phrase.
Drill: Practice top-bottom-top stick hits on counts 1-2-3.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: On count 1 of refrain, women strike right stick to the top of the man's long stick.
Step 4: On count 2, women strike left stick to the bottom of the man's long stick.
Drill: Practice turning on count 4 to reset position.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid misaligned stick strikes to ensure safety during rapid four-beat contact patterns.
